title: Deterministic simulation and trace validation
objective: Find and name the first divergence between two runs of one seed; mark each log line as a spec action, a stuttering step or the first line no behavior matches; and find the first non-conforming line of a mutant that passes the suite, and name its drift.

blocks.md: Your simulator can replay any failure from a seed, and your spec says which steps are allowed. This lesson joins them. The simulator writes a log, TLC checks that the log is a behavior of your spec, and a mutant that passes every test in the course's suite fails on its first wrong line.

choice.prompt: Two runs of your simulator with the same seed produce different traces. Where do you look first?

options.text: At what the seed does not fix: a clock, an unseeded random source, a host order.
options.why: Determinism means every choice comes from the seed and the inputs.

options.text: At the seed: it is too small, and two runs of one seed can drift apart.
options.why: Any seed replays exactly if every random choice derives from it.

options.text: Nowhere: faults are random, by design, and two runs of one seed differ.
options.why: Seeded randomness is reproducible. That is what a seed is for.

choice.prompt: Trace validation accepts the traces of n seeds. What does that establish?

options.text: Your implementation is right on every input, logged or not.
options.why: It covers these n traces, at the logged detail, against the spec you wrote.

options.text: Your implementation agrees with a reference implementation.
options.why: That is differential testing. Here the oracle is a spec that allows many behaviors.

options.text: Each of those n traces is a behavior of your spec, at the logged detail.
options.why: It is membership, trace by trace, and says nothing about traces never run.

options.text: Your spec is right about your system, at the logged detail.
options.why: The spec and the code can share one misreading.

blocks.md: Your machine is sans-I/O: `step(&mut self, input) -> Vec<Output>`. It has no clock, no randomness and no network, and the zero-import ABI gives it no way to reach them. The harness owns time, faults, the simulated world and the log. So a run is a function of the machine and the seed: replay it and you get the same trace, byte for byte.
Run the reference machine on recorded seed 1 twice. The cell prints both trace hashes. Then run a harness variant that draws its faults from an unseeded host source.
blocks.direction: Run asserts: the same seed gives the same trace. Equal hashes mean byte-identical traces.

call.prompt: With the planted variant, which component can make two runs of seed 1 differ?

options.text: The machine, as it ran twice.
options.why: With no imports, the same inputs give the same outputs, step after step.

options.text: TLC, as it checked both runs.
options.why: TLC reads traces. It does not produce them.

options.text: The harness's fault plan.
options.why: It chose faults from a source the seed does not control.

blocks.after: The reference traces are byte-identical, and the variant's traces differ at a reported line {{run:RUN-sim-determinism}}. A failing seed is now a bug report: replay it exactly, then shrink the fault schedule until every remaining fault matters. WebAssembly has nondeterminism of its own (NaN bit patterns, resource exhaustion); this lab's integer-only machine stays clear of it.

choice.prompt: Two runs of seed 7 write the same first three lines. Line 4 is `Timeout c1` in one run and `Receive c1` in the other. The harness fires a timer when the host clock passes a threshold. What is the first diverging line, and what is its source?

options.text: Line 3, the machine's last step before the split.
options.why: The runs agree through line 3, and a machine with no imports cannot differ on equal inputs.

options.text: Line 4, a timer input driven by the wall clock.
options.why: The host clock is not derived from the seed, so two runs fire the timer at different points.

options.text: Line 4, a fault drawn from an unseeded source.
options.why: A fault plan could diverge like this, but here the timer comes from the clock.

blocks.direction: Check asserts: the log is a behavior of the spec. Accepted means some behavior consumes every line. Rejected names the first line that no behavior consumes.

code.text:
\* run: statespace trace validate spec/Outbox.tla traces/seed-1.ndjson
---- MODULE OutboxTrace ----
EXTENDS Outbox, TraceValidation

IsCommit   == IsEvent("Commit") /\ Line.cmd \in Cmds /\ Commit(Line.cmd)

IsDispatch == /\ IsEvent("Dispatch")
              /\ Line.cmd \in Cmds
              /\ Dispatch(Line.cmd)
              /\ \E r \in reqs' \ reqs :
                    /\ Logged("key") => r.key = Line.key
                    /\ Logged("att") => r.att = Line.att

IsReceive  == IsEvent("Receive") /\ Line.cmd \in Cmds /\ Receive(Line.cmd)
IsPersist  == IsEvent("Persist") /\ Line.cmd \in Cmds /\ Persist(Line.cmd)
IsAck      == IsEvent("Ack")     /\ Line.cmd \in Cmds /\ Ack(Line.cmd)
IsCrash    == IsEvent("Crash")   /\ Crash
IsRecover  == IsEvent("Recover") /\ Recover

\* An implementation-only line is a stuttering step: no spec variable changes.
IsTimer    == IsEvent("TimerArmed") /\ UNCHANGED vars
IsEnd      == IsEvent("End") /\ IsLast /\ UNCHANGED vars

\* The provider's Accept is not logged, so TLC searches for it.
ProviderStep == Unlogged /\ \E r \in reqs : Accept(r)

TraceInit == Init /\ l = 1
TraceNext == \/ IsCommit \/ IsDispatch \/ IsReceive \/ IsPersist \/ IsAck
             \/ IsCrash \/ IsRecover \/ IsTimer \/ IsEnd \/ ProviderStep
TraceSpec == TraceInit /\ [][TraceNext]_<<vars, l>>
====

call.prompt: A log line records a timer being armed between Dispatch and Accept. Is the trace accepted?

options.text: Accepted: the line is a stuttering step.
options.why: Specs allow stuttering so that steps the spec cannot see are permitted.

options.text: Rejected: each line must be a spec action.
options.why: The stuttering disjunct matches the line with every spec variable unchanged.

options.text: Accepted, if the deadlock check is on.
options.why: The deadlock check decides whether a stuck state is reported. Acceptance means every line was consumed.

blocks.after: Two cautions from the paper. Too little logged information causes state explosion or wrongly accepted traces (§4.5). And a rejection yields no counterexample, only a maximal matching behavior (§4.2), so the tool reports the highest line any behavior reached. TLC's search depth equals that line only when every step consumes one, and the provider's unlogged steps consume none {{run:RUN-tlc-tracemodule}}. TLC's trace-loading option is not needed: it replays traces that TLC itself wrote, not an implementation's log, and the pinned jar's `Json` module reads the log through `ndJsonDeserialize` {{run:RUN-tlc-tracemodule}}.

choice.prompt: A log reads: 1 Commit c1; 2 Dispatch c1; 3 TimerArmed; 4 Persist c1; 5 End. Which description is right?

options.text: Line 3 is the first line no behavior matches: a timer is not a spec action.
options.why: The stuttering disjunct matches line 3 with every spec variable unchanged.

options.text: Every line is a spec action or a stuttering step, so the log is accepted.
options.why: A line that fits on its own can still fail in order. Persist has no reply to store.

options.text: Line 3 is a stuttering step, and line 4 is the first line no behavior matches.
options.why: Persist needs a received reply, and the log shows no Receive. TLC can add the provider's Accept but not the worker's Receive.

blocks.md: A mutant of the reference simulator marks the intent done before it stores the provider's result. The course's end-state suite checks that every committed intent is acknowledged and that an idempotent provider is never double-charged. The mutant passes it on every recorded seed. Then trace validation reads the same seeds' traces.

blocks.direction: Check asserts: the log is a behavior of the spec. Rejected names the first line that no behavior consumes.

call.prompt: The mutant passes the suite on every recorded seed. Will trace validation accept its fault-free traces?

options.text: Accepted: no crash, no harm.
options.why: The spec orders Persist before Ack, and the order is wrong on every trace, crash or no crash.

options.text: Rejected at the first Ack line.
options.why: Ack is not enabled before the result is stored, so no behavior matches that line.

options.text: Rejected only on seeds that crash between Ack and Persist.
options.why: That is how a test would find it. Trace validation checks the steps, not their consequences.

blocks.after: The suite checks outcomes, and outcomes agree whenever no crash lands between the two steps. Trace validation checks the order of steps on every trace, so it sees the drift before a crash makes it costly. This is specimen SP-8.4 {{run:RUN-tlc-trace-validation}}. It also mints CL-8.3: TESTED [T] · n seeds, composed with the spec's MODEL-CHECKED [M] result. The simulated environment stays ASSUMED [A].

choice.prompt: Which is the first line no behavior of the spec matches, and which drift is it?

options.text: Line 6: a new key for the second attempt.
options.why: The spec's key names the intent, so the re-send must carry the key of line 2.

options.text: Line 3: a Receive with no Accept logged before it.
options.why: The provider's Accept is not logged, so TLC searches for it. A Receive after a Dispatch is allowed.

options.text: Line 4: the crash.
options.why: A reply is in flight and unstored, so a crash is enabled. The environment's steps are in the spec.

options.text: None: the end state is fine, so the log conforms.
options.why: The outcome agrees, but the key does not. A test that checks outcomes would miss it.

choice.prompt: A log reads: 1 Commit c1; 2 Dispatch c1; 3 Receive c1; 4 TimerArmed; 5 Persist c1; 6 Ack c1; 7 End. Which description is right?

options.text: Line 4: a stuttering step, and the log is accepted.
options.why: Line 3 fits because TLC adds the provider's Accept before it. Every other line is a spec action or a stuttering step, in order.

options.text: Line 3 is the first line no behavior matches: no Accept is logged.
options.why: The provider's Accept is unlogged, and TLC searches for it.

options.text: Line 4 is the first line no behavior matches: a timer is not a spec action.
options.why: A step that changes no spec variable is a stuttering step.

choice.prompt: Two runs of seed 9 write the same lines, except that after a crash and a recovery the replies for c1 and c2 appear as c1 then c2 in one run and c2 then c1 in the other. The harness delivers the batch from a hash map. What is the source?

options.text: The machine reordered its outputs.
options.why: With no imports, the same inputs give the same outputs.

options.text: A host-ordered delivery of a reply batch.
options.why: The map's iteration order is chosen by the host, not derived from the seed.

options.text: TLC explored the replies in another order.
options.why: TLC reads the traces. It does not produce them.

blocks.md: The byzantine course applies the same discipline to a cluster: seeded random streams and harness-driven timers, in a deterministic network harness. Drawer D-21 is its self-contained prerequisite. Raft and partitions stay in byzantine.

blocks.title: CCF: smart casual verification
blocks.md: Howard et al., NSDI 2025 ([arXiv 2406.17455](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17455), v2, 2024-10-16): §6 Trace Validation (§6.1, §6.2.1 Aligning Grains Of Atomicity, §6.3) and §7 Results (six consensus bugs, five safety and one liveness), run in CCF's CI. Trace three questions at the commit pinned in {{run:RUN-twin-pins}}: the trace module's line counter, where it aligns a coarser grain of atomicity, and how CI decides a trace failed.

blocks.title: TigerBeetle: the VOPR
blocks.md: TigerBeetle's Safety page (read 2026-10-23) describes a cluster "running real code" that meets "network, storage and process faults, at 1000x speed". Trace three questions against your harness: where a seed fixes the fault schedule, how a failing seed replays, and where invariants are checked. The simulator at [sim.tigerbeetle.com](https://sim.tigerbeetle.com) is a link-out to TigerBeetle's own page, outside this course.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Cirstea et al. ([arXiv 2404.16075](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16075)): §3 Instrumenting Distributed Programs; §4.2 Realizing trace validation using the TLC model checker; §4.3 Analyzing discrepancies; §4.5 Implementation aspects (v2, 2024-09-17).

blocks.title: Reading: the limit of trace checking
blocks.md: Davis, Hirschhorn and Schvimer, "eXtreme Modelling in Practice", PVLDB 13(9):1346–1358, 2020 ([arXiv 2006.00915](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.00915), 2020-05-28). Its abstract reports: "We found MBTC to be impractical for testing that the Server conformed to a highly abstract specification." Log at your spec's grain.

The planted variant (--planted-unseeded) is S8.L6's: the harness's fault plan draws from Python's SystemRandom, which the seed does not control. Its traces differ from run to run by design, so its outputs are informational; the comparison line is the evidence.
cmp's line is copied as it printed it; for byte-identical files cmp prints nothing and exits 0, and the record says so in words.

The reference simulator in bench/statespace/sim.py is a port of LAB-8's Rust harness (labs/LAB-8/sim/src/world.rs) with the course's reference machine; for the same machine and seed the two write the same bytes (checked by hand over 25 seeds and three mutants while building LAB-8, not recorded here).

Each configuration's verdict lines are the lines statespace trace validate printed, one per trace and a summary; TLC's whole output for each trace stays in the tool's scratch folder, and the tool reads the verdict from the trace-validation record TraceValidation.tla prints, never from TLC's exit code [X RUN-tlc-tracemodule].

The n-seeds configuration validates against RUN-tlc-trace-drift's Outbox.tla and OutboxIface.tla, already in the registry, with that run's trace module plus one disjunct for the Timeout lines LAB-8's harness writes. LAB-8.6 itself validates the learner's own machine against the learner's own spec.
The trace generators are configurations with engine statespace-sim (bench/statespace/sim.py, the reference simulator), so each trace's bytes trace back to a command.

notes: Question: does the trace-module method of Cirstea, Kuppe, Loillier and Merz (section 4.2), as CCF applies it, validate NDJSON traces on the pinned 1.8.0 jar with only its bundled modules, and what does it report for an accepted, a rejected and a partial trace? docs/spikes/W0-S13.md answers it from the configurations below.

The spec is a toy outbox written for this spike (scripts/spikes/W0-S13/specs/ToyOutbox.tla), not the course's reference model, which W5-T02 authors. Its traces are written by hand in the shape a simulator would emit; no simulator exists yet (W5-T15).

Every TLC run was in a fresh container with no network, on one Linux x86_64 host. Nothing is emulated. A run takes well under two seconds, most of it container and JVM start-up, so duration_s says little about TLC itself; TLC printed "Finished in 00s" for every trace run.

TLC unpacks its standard modules to a fresh /tmp/tlc-<n> directory inside the container; the committed stdout writes that directory as <tlc-temp>. The binary trace of replay-dump has a generated name (ToyOutboxReplay_TTrace_<n>.bin) and is loaded by replay-bin as replay.bin.
Outputs marked informational hold a random seed, timestamps or a generated file name, so a re-run is compared on the configs, traces, state lists and verdict_lines only.

The typo-* configs replace one text in a copy of ToyOutboxTrace.tla before TLC runs, as a learner's slip would; the edited copy is saved with their outputs. They and accepted-174 and composed-no-flag show what the tool prints when TLC stops without a verdict line: SANY's message or the exception's, not TLC's first Error: line, which for these stops is generic.

notes: Recorded by W1 follow-up 1 (task_label W1-followup-1); the task field is left out because run@1 accepts only W<n>-S<nn> or W<n>-T<nn> there.
A pin is the commit a ref pointed to when ls-remote read it; read_at is that instant. The record is stale 60 days after its started_at and is refreshed by re-running the commands in argv.

git ls-remote was first run with several ref patterns per command (HEAD plus refs/tags/... or refs/heads/...); for leanprover/lean4 and postgres/postgres that printed nothing with exit 0. The recorded run uses one pattern per command; the pin for lean4 tags and PR 14577 uses a trailing * pattern, and every matching ref is kept in refs.

refs/pull/14577/merge is not advertised; only refs/pull/14577/head is. The v4.35.0 tag points at eb6cafb7290e8bd5f2937522d8d804f58f02bafc, the commit the bench image's Lean prints in its version string.

Twin cards that name no git repository are not pinned here: Stripe's "Idempotent requests" API page, the Zanzibar paper (USENIX ATC 2019), Jepsen's PostgreSQL 12.3 analysis, the arXiv papers on Cedar and CCF, SymCert (FMCAD 2026) and the AWS Automated Reasoning checks pages. Each card states its own read date.
Isabelle is developed in Mercurial; the pin is from its GitHub mirror, isabelle-prover/mirror-isabelle.
